name_en: Da Wu Ye Dancong (Big Dark Leaf)
cultivar: Fenghuang Shui Xian, Da Wu Ye strain
processing: Sun-withered, shaken firmly overnight to a medium oxidation, fixed, rolled into long strips and charcoal roasted light to medium; the large, dark leaf stands a solid roast.
harvest_season: Spring, April into early May; a vigorous mid-season strain picked once, with some gardens taking a small autumn lot.
appearance_dry: Long, broad, dark brown to near-black strips, heavier and darker than most dancong, with a strong floral-honey smell.
appearance_wet: Large, thick, dark olive leaves with red edges, the darkest wet leaf of the family.
taste_profile: A bold floral-and-honey aroma with ripe fruit, a thick body with a slight bitter edge that turns to a long sweetness, and a strong, cooling finish that lasts.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps. It is strong: use a touch less leaf than for Mi Lan Xiang and pour fast, and it will reward you with nine or ten infusions.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually from early summer for light roasts and from autumn for medium roasts and high-mountain lots. Its thick leaf keeps well: two to four years sealed and dry, and it is one of the dancongs that improves with a few months of rest after roasting.
description:
Da Wu Ye, big dark leaf, is the Phoenix dancong named for the plant rather than the perfume: a vigorous strain with large, dark leaves that makes a bold, thick, honey-floral oolong with real staying power. It has become one of the most popular strains in Chaozhou in recent years because it delivers aroma and body together.

It descends, like all dancong, from a selected single tree of the Fenghuang Shui Xian population, chosen in this case for its big dark foliage and generous aroma, and it is now grown widely from the low gardens around Fenghuang town up to the high slopes. It is not one of the ten classic aroma types; its fragrance is usually described as a mix of orchid, honey and ripe fruit rather than a single flower.

The leaf is withered, shaken firmly overnight to a medium oxidation and rolled into long strips, then charcoal roasted, and because the leaf is thick makers can give it a proper roast without hollowing it out. The cup is deep gold, the aroma is bold and floral, the body is thick with honey and fruit, and there is a frank bitter edge at the front that turns into a long, cool sweetness, the hui gan that Chaozhou drinkers judge a tea by.

Brew it with slightly less leaf than a Mi Lan Xiang, boiling water and genuinely fast pours; it is a strong tea, and a slow hand gets bitterness without the sweetness. Brewed well it runs nine or ten steeps and the later ones are the best.

It is sold by year with elevation stated, and it is good value: because it is not a classic name, high-mountain Da Wu Ye often costs less than a comparable Mi Lan Xiang while giving more body. It rests well and keeps for a few years. If you like it, Ba Xian is the next tea up the bitterness-and-sweetness ladder, and a Wudong lao cong of any type is the next up in depth.
sources_note: Da Wu Ye is variously said to originate on Wudong or elsewhere in the Fenghuang range; no specific village is stated.
